idiom_name: v.shrink_to_fit() (and v.shrink_to(min_capacity) as the regrowth guard)
implementation_notes: Vec and String carry the operation as a method: shrink_to_fit 'shrinks the capacity of the vector as much as possible', but 'the behavior of this method depends on the allocator, which may either shrink the vector in-place or reallocate' and 'the resulting vector might still have some excess capacity'. It is the default because the type and the growth capability survive; Rust never shrinks a vector implicitly - even an emptied Vec keeps its allocation until it is dropped - so this call is the only way to hand unused capacity back while staying growable. shrink_to(min_capacity) (stable since 1.56) is the same call with a floor: 'The capacity will remain at least as large as both the length and the supplied value', which keeps a container that regrows from thrashing.
pitfalls: Any &T/&mut T, slice or raw pointer taken from the vector before the call dangles if it reallocates - the borrow checker blocks the safe version, but pointers laundered through unsafe code or slices split off earlier are not protected.
It is a request, not a guarantee: the allocator may keep the allocation or only partially shrink it, so capacity() can stay above len() - do not build a memory budget on it.
Calling it after every mutation is a pessimization: the next push reallocates immediately, converting amortized O(1) growth into repeated copies - trim once, at the end of the growth phase.
String::shrink_to_fit has the same shape; on a String that still shares nothing it is a no-op, but a String with slack copies when it reallocates.

If you wish to free up unused memory, use shrink_to_fit or shrink_to'; method docs: shrink_to_fit 'Shrinks the capacity of the vector as much as possible. The behavior of this method depends on the allocator, which may either shrink the vector in-place or reallocate. The resulting vector might still have some excess capacity'; shrink_to: 'Shrinks the capacity of the vector with a lower bound. The capacity will remain at least as large as both the length and the supplied value': https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html

variants.name: Vec::into_boxed_slice() (exact shape, no further growth)
variants.implementation_notes: When the container is finished, converting it pins the shape instead of asking for a favour: into_boxed_slice removes any excess capacity and yields a Box<[T]> whose capacity equals its length, and the conversion is in-place when len == capacity (otherwise it reallocates). The price is the growth capability - Box<[T]> has no push - so it is the right variant for data handed out as a fixed buffer (serialized output, lookup tables, FFI) and the wrong one for a working container; converting back with Vec::from may reallocate again. Use it when 'this buffer is exactly this size now' is the actual statement you want to make in the type system.
pitfalls: The conversion changes the type: a later append means Vec::from(frozen), which may reallocate and copy again.
It is not free when the vector is over-allocated: the excess is removed by reallocating and copying, with both allocations live during the conversion.
Box<[T]> is a uniquely owned fixed-length value, not a cheap shared view - cloning it clones the elements, so it is the wrong shape for a buffer that many owners should reference.
sources: doc.rust-lang.org, Vec::into_boxed_slice - 'Any excess capacity is removed', with the example that a Vec::with_capacity(10) holding three elements yields a boxed slice whose into_vec().capacity() is 3; the Vec overview notes the conversion is in-place when len == capacity: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.into_boxed_slice
